title: Random Variables
description: Discrete and continuous random variables, PMFs, PDFs and CDFs, from bit-error counts to Gaussian noise and the Q-function.

study.title: Random variables and the CDF
study.body: A **random variable** $X$ assigns a number to every outcome: the number of bit errors in a packet, a noise voltage, the value of a resistor taken from a reel. Its **cumulative distribution function** $F_X(x) = P(X \le x)$ describes it completely: $F_X$ rises from 0 to 1, never decreases, and gives the probability of any interval as a difference.

study.title: Discrete RVs: Bernoulli and binomial
study.body: A discrete RV takes countable values with probabilities $p_X(k) = P(X = k)$ (the **PMF**), which sum to 1. **Bernoulli**: a single trial, $P(X = 1) = p$, e.g. one bit in error. **Binomial**: the number of successes in $n$ independent Bernoulli trials, e.g. the bit errors in an $n$-bit word. Drag $n$ and $p$: the PMF peaks near $np$.

study.title: Geometric and Poisson RVs
study.body: **Geometric**: the number of independent trials up to and including the first success, $P(K = k) = (1-p)^{k-1}p$ for $k \ge 1$, e.g. the transmissions needed to get a packet through. **Poisson**: the number of events in an interval when they occur independently at an average rate $\lambda$, with $\alpha = \lambda T$ expected events: packets at a router, photons at a detector, radiation-induced bit flips. It also approximates the binomial for large $n$ and small $p$, with $\alpha = np$. Drag $\alpha$.

study.title: Continuous RVs: uniform and exponential
study.body: A continuous RV has a **probability density function** $f_X(x) = dF_X/dx$: probabilities are areas under it, and $P(X = a) = 0$ for any single value. **Uniform** on $(a, b)$: $f_X = 1/(b-a)$, e.g. the rounding error of an ADC on $(-\Delta/2, \Delta/2)$. **Exponential** with rate $\lambda$: $f_T(t) = \lambda e^{-\lambda t}$ for $t \ge 0$, the waiting time between Poisson events or the lifetime of a part with a constant failure rate. It is **memoryless**: a part that has survived so far is as good as new. Drag $\lambda$.

study.title: The Gaussian random variable
study.body: Thermal noise, sums of many small effects and component spreads are well modelled by the **Gaussian** (normal) density $\mathcal{N}(\mu, \sigma^2)$: a bell centred on the mean $\mu$ whose width is set by the standard deviation $\sigma$. About 68 % of the probability lies within $\mu \pm \sigma$, 95 % within $\mu \pm 2\sigma$ and 99.7 % within $\mu \pm 3\sigma$. Drag the threshold $a$: the orange tail beyond it has probability $Q((a-\mu)/\sigma)$.

study.title: The Q-function
study.body: The Gaussian CDF has no closed form, so tail probabilities are written with $Q(z) = P(Z > z)$ for a **standard** Gaussian $Z$ (mean 0, $\sigma$ = 1). Standardize any Gaussian with $z = (x-\mu)/\sigma$. Values to know: $Q(0) = 0.5$, $Q(1) = 0.159$, $Q(1.28) = 0.10$, $Q(1.645) = 0.05$, $Q(2) = 0.0228$, $Q(2.33) = 0.01$, $Q(3) = 1.35\times10^{-3}$. Symmetry: $Q(-z) = 1 - Q(z)$. On a calculator, $Q(z) = 1 - \Phi(z)$ (normal CDF) $= \tfrac12\,\mathrm{erfc}(z/\sqrt2)$. Drag $z$: the tail falls faster and faster.

study.title: Worked example: resistor tolerance
study.body: A process makes resistors with $\mu$ = 1000 Ω and $\sigma$ = 10 Ω, sold as 1 kΩ ± 2 %. The limits 980 Ω and 1020 Ω lie $z = 20/10 = 2$ standard deviations from the mean, so $P(\text{out of spec}) = 2Q(2) = 0.0455$: 4.6 % are rejected. With $\sigma$ = 5 Ω the limits are at $4\sigma$ and only $2Q(4) = 6.3\times10^{-5}$ fall outside.

steps.title: Random variables and PMFs
steps.body: A **random variable** maps each outcome to a number. A discrete RV has a probability mass function $p_X(k) = P(X = k)$, with $\sum_k p_X(k) = 1$. The simplest is the **Bernoulli** RV: 1 with probability $p$ (say, a bit error), 0 otherwise. Counting the errors among $n$ independent bits gives a **binomial** RV.

steps.prompt: A word of {{n}} bits crosses a channel that flips each bit independently with probability {{p}}. What is the probability that the number of bit errors in the word is exactly {{k}}? (probability, 0–1)
steps.explanation: The number of errors $K$ is binomial: $P(K = {{k}}) = \binom{{{n}}}{{{k}}}p^{{{k}}}(1-p)^{{{n-k}}}$ = {{choose(n,k)}} × {{p^k}} × {{(1-p)^(n-k)}} = **{{choose(n,k)*p^k*(1-p)^(n-k)}}**.

steps.title: The geometric RV
steps.body: A link repeats a packet until it gets through, and each attempt succeeds independently with probability $q$. The number of attempts $K$ is **geometric**: $k - 1$ failures followed by one success. More than $m$ attempts are needed exactly when the first $m$ all fail.

steps.prompt: Each transmission of a packet succeeds independently with probability {{q}}; the sender repeats until it succeeds.

ask.prompt: What is the probability that exactly {{k}} transmissions are needed? (probability, 0–1)
What is the probability that more than {{m}} transmissions are needed? (probability, 0–1)
ask.explanation: More than {{m}} attempts means the first {{m}} all failed: $(1-q)^{m}$ = $({{1-q}})^{{{m}}}$ = **{{(1-q)^m}}**.

steps.title: The Poisson RV
steps.body: Events that occur independently at an average rate $\lambda$ (packets at a router, photons at a photodiode, radiation-induced bit flips) give a **Poisson** count in an interval $T$, with $\alpha = \lambda T$ events expected.

steps.prompt: Packets arrive at a router as a Poisson stream with an average rate of {{lam}} packets/s. What is the probability that the number of packets arriving in {{T|s}} is exactly {{k}}? (probability, 0–1)
steps.explanation: Expected count: $\alpha = \lambda T$ = {{lam}} × {{T|s}} = {{lam*T}}. Then $P(N = {{k}}) = \frac{\alpha^{{{k}}}}{{{k}}!}e^{-\alpha}$ = **{{(lam*T)^k*exp(-lam*T)/fact(k)}}**.

steps.prompt: Match each random variable to a situation it models
pairs: Whether one bit is received in error
Number of bit errors in a 64-bit word
Number of transmissions until a packet gets through
Number of packets arriving at a router in 1 ms
steps.explanation: Bernoulli: one yes/no trial. Binomial: the number of successes in a fixed number $n$ of independent trials. Geometric: the number of trials up to the first success. Poisson: the number of independent events in a fixed time interval, with no upper limit.

steps.prompt: Each of 10 bits is flipped independently with probability {{p}}. Which stem plot shows the PMF of the number of bit errors $K$?
steps.explanation: $K$ is binomial with $n$ = 10 and $p$ = {{p}}, so its PMF peaks near the mean $np$ = {{10*p}} errors. The mirrored plot (peak near {{10-10*p}}) counts the **correct** bits instead, and the symmetric plot belongs to $p$ = 0.5.

steps.title: PDF and the uniform RV
steps.body: A continuous RV is described by its probability density $f_X(x)$: the probability of an interval is the area under $f_X$ over that interval, and the total area is 1. The **uniform** RV on $(a, b)$ has the flat density $1/(b-a)$. Example: the rounding error of an ideal ADC is uniform between $-\Delta/2$ and $+\Delta/2$ (Δ = 1 LSB).

steps.prompt: The rounding error of an ADC is uniform between −Δ/2 and +Δ/2, with Δ = {{D|V}}. What is the probability that the error magnitude is below {{cc|V}}? (probability, 0–1)
steps.explanation: The density is $1/\Delta$ over a width Δ. The event $|e| < c$ is the interval from −{{cc|V}} to +{{cc|V}}, of width {{2*cc|V}}: $P = 2c/\Delta$ = {{2*cc|V}} / {{D|V}} = **{{2*cc/D}}**.

steps.title: The exponential RV
steps.body: Lifetimes of parts with a constant failure rate, and waiting times between Poisson events, are **exponential** with rate $\lambda$ (mean $1/\lambda$). The survival probability decays exponentially, and the distribution is **memoryless**: having survived until now does not change the chances for the next $t$ seconds.
steps.formula: \begin{aligned} f_T(t) &= \lambda e^{-\lambda t} \\ P(T > t) &= e^{-\lambda t} \end{aligned}

steps.prompt: An LED driver has an exponentially distributed lifetime with a mean (MTTF) of {{m|h}}. What is the probability that it still works after {{t|h}}? (probability, 0–1)
steps.explanation: $\lambda = 1/\text{MTTF}$, so $P(T > t) = e^{-t/\text{MTTF}}$ = $e^{-{{t/m}}}$ = **{{exp(-t/m)}}**.

steps.title: The Gaussian RV and the Q-function
steps.body: A Gaussian RV $X \sim \mathcal{N}(\mu, \sigma^2)$ is standardized by $Z = (X-\mu)/\sigma$, a Gaussian with mean 0 and $\sigma$ = 1. Its upper tail is the **Q-function**, $Q(z) = P(Z > z)$ (orange: the tail beyond $z$). Values to remember: $Q(1) = 0.159$, $Q(1.28) = 0.10$, $Q(1.645) = 0.05$, $Q(2) = 0.023$, $Q(2.33) = 0.01$, $Q(3) = 0.0013$. By symmetry $Q(-z) = 1 - Q(z)$; on a calculator, $Q(z) = 1 - \Phi(z)$ (normal CDF).

steps.prompt: The noise voltage at an amplifier output is Gaussian with mean 0 and $\sigma$ = {{sig|V}}. What is the probability that at a given instant it exceeds {{a|V}}? (probability, 0–1)
steps.explanation: Standardize: $z = a/\sigma$ = {{a|V}} / {{sig|V}} = {{a/sig}}. Then $P(V > a) = Q({{a/sig}})$ = **{{Q(a/sig)}}**.

steps.prompt: Gaussian noise has zero mean and $\sigma$ = {{sig|V}}. What is the probability that its magnitude exceeds {{a|V}}, i.e. $P(|V| > a)$?
steps.explanation: Both tails count, and by symmetry they are equal: $P(|V| > a) = 2Q(a/\sigma)$ = 2Q({{k}}) = **{{2*Q(k)}}**. $Q$ alone is one tail; $1 - 2Q$ is the probability of staying **inside** ±{{a|V}}.

steps.prompt: A sensor output is Gaussian with mean {{mu|V}} and $\sigma$ = {{sig|V}}. An alarm trips when it exceeds the threshold $a$. Set $a$ so that the false-alarm probability $P(X > a)$ is {{tgt}}.
steps.hint: Find $z$ with $Q(z)$ = {{tgt}} (values in the previous steps), then $a = \mu + z\sigma$.
steps.explanation: Look up the $z$ with $Q(z)$ = {{tgt}}: $z$ = {{zt}}. Then $a = \mu + z\sigma$ = {{mu|V}} + {{zt}} × {{sig|V}} = **{{at|V}}**.

steps.prompt: For a continuous random variable, $P(X = a) = 0$ for every single value $a$, even where the PDF $f_X(a)$ is large.
steps.explanation: A probability is an area under the PDF, and a single point has zero width. $f_X(a)$ is a density: $P(a < X \le a + \Delta x) \approx f_X(a)\,\Delta x$ for a small interval. A density can even exceed 1: a uniform PDF on (0, 0.1) equals 10.

steps.prompt: A process makes resistors with mean {{R0|Ω}} and standard deviation {{sig|Ω}} (Gaussian). What fraction falls **outside** the ±{{100*tol}}% tolerance band? (probability, 0–1)
steps.explanation: The band edges are {{tol*R0|Ω}} from the mean, i.e. $k$ = {{tol*R0|Ω}} / {{sig|Ω}} = {{k}} standard deviations. Both tails count: $2Q(k)$ = 2Q({{k}}) = **{{2*Q(k)}}**.

steps.prompt: Single-event upsets (bit flips caused by radiation) hit a memory as a Poisson process with an average of {{r}} per day. What is the probability of at least one upset in {{d}} days? (probability, 0–1)
steps.explanation: Expected number: $\alpha = \lambda T$ = {{r}} × {{d}} = {{r*d}}. 'At least one' is the complement of 'none': $1 - P(N = 0) = 1 - e^{-\alpha}$ = **{{1-exp(-r*d)}}**.

steps.prompt: The time between bursts of interference on a bus is exponential with mean {{mT|s}}. No burst has occurred during the last {{t1|s}}. What is the probability that none occurs in the next {{t2|s}}?
steps.explanation: The exponential distribution is **memoryless**: $P(T > t_1 + t_2 \mid T > t_1) = \frac{e^{-(t_1+t_2)/m}}{e^{-t_1/m}} = e^{-t_2/m}$ = **{{exp(-t2/mT)}}**. The {{t1|s}} already waited does not matter; {{exp(-(t1+t2)/mT)}} would be the probability of no burst during the whole {{t1+t2|s}} from the start.

steps.prompt: A 5 V rail has a Gaussian error: mean {{mu|V}}, $\sigma$ = {{sig|V}}. A monitor flags the rail when a reading is below {{lo|V}} or above {{hi|V}}. What is the probability that a reading is flagged? (probability, 0–1)
steps.explanation: Standardize both limits: $z_{lo}$ = ({{mu|V}} − {{lo|V}}) / {{sig|V}} = {{(mu-lo)/sig}} and $z_{hi}$ = ({{hi|V}} − {{mu|V}}) / {{sig|V}} = {{(hi-mu)/sig}}. The two tails are disjoint, so add them: $Q({{(mu-lo)/sig}}) + Q({{(hi-mu)/sig}})$ = {{Q((mu-lo)/sig)}} + {{Q((hi-mu)/sig)}} = **{{Q((mu-lo)/sig)+Q((hi-mu)/sig)}}**.

steps.prompt: A board uses {{n}} identical ICs, each defective with probability {{p}}, independently. What is the probability that two or more ICs on a board are defective? (probability, 0–1)
Which graph can be the cumulative distribution function $F_X(x)$ of a random variable? (The dashed line is at 1.)
steps.explanation: A CDF $F_X(x) = P(X \le x)$ starts at 0, **never decreases** (a larger $x$ can only include more outcomes) and approaches 1. The exponential CDF $1 - e^{-x}$ does exactly that. A curve that goes down somewhere or rises above 1 cannot be a CDF; the decaying curve looks like an exponential **PDF**.

steps.prompt: A comparator should output high because its input is a DC level of {{mu|V}}, but Gaussian noise with $\sigma$ = {{sig|V}} is added. What is the probability that at a given instant the input is below 0 V (a wrong output)? (probability, 0–1)
steps.explanation: $P(X < 0) = P\!\left(Z < \frac{0-\mu}{\sigma}\right) = Q(\mu/\sigma)$ by symmetry, with $\mu/\sigma$ = {{mu|V}} / {{sig|V}} = {{mu/sig}}: **{{Q(mu/sig)}}**.

steps.prompt: For a Gaussian random variable, $P(|X - \mu| > {{k}}\sigma)$ is below 1 %.

A bit is sent as +{{A|V}} (a 1) or −{{A|V}} (a 0). The receiver adds Gaussian noise with $\sigma$ = {{sig|V}} and decides '1' when the sample is positive. What is the probability that a sent 1 is decoded as 0? (probability, 0–1)
steps.explanation: A sent 1 gives $X = A + N$, Gaussian with mean {{A|V}}. An error needs $X < 0$, i.e. $N < -A$: $P = Q(A/\sigma)$ = Q({{A/sig}}) = **{{Q(A/sig)}}**. By symmetry a sent 0 fails equally often.

steps.prompt: Resistors of nominal value {{R0|Ω}} are specified at ±{{100*tol}}%. The process is centred and Gaussian. What is the largest standard deviation $\sigma$ that keeps at most 0.2 % of the parts outside the tolerance band? Use $Q(3.09) = 0.001$.
steps.explanation: Out of tolerance means beyond $\pm k\sigma$, with probability $2Q(k)$. Setting $2Q(k)$ = 0.002 gives $Q(k)$ = 0.001, so $k$ = 3.09: the band half-width {{tol*R0|Ω}} must be at least 3.09 σ. $\sigma$ = {{tol*R0|Ω}} / 3.09 = **{{tol*R0/3.09|Ω}}**.

steps.prompt: A resistor process should be centred on 1 kΩ but has drifted to a mean of {{mu||4}} Ω, with $\sigma$ = {{sig}} Ω (Gaussian). The spec is 1 kΩ ± 1 % (990 Ω to 1010 Ω). What fraction is out of spec? (probability, 0–1)
steps.explanation: Upper margin: (1010 − {{mu||4}}) / {{sig}} = {{(1010-mu)/sig}} σ; lower margin: ({{mu||4}} − 990) / {{sig}} = {{(mu-990)/sig}} σ. Out of spec: $Q({{(1010-mu)/sig}}) + Q({{(mu-990)/sig}})$ = {{Q((1010-mu)/sig)}} + {{Q((mu-990)/sig)}} = **{{Q((1010-mu)/sig)+Q((mu-990)/sig)}}**. Centred, it would be only 2Q({{10/sig}}) = {{2*Q(10/sig)}}: the drift costs far more than it seems.

steps.prompt: An optical receiver decides '1' when at least one photon is detected during the bit. Photon counts are Poisson, and the transmitter is dark for a 0 (no photons at all).

ask.prompt: A 1 pulse delivers on average {{al}} photons. What is the probability that a sent 1 is missed? (probability, 0–1)
ask.explanation: A 1 is missed only if zero photons arrive: $P(N = 0) = e^{-\alpha}$ = $e^{-{{al}}}$ = **{{exp(-al)}}**.

ask.prompt: How many photons must a 1 pulse deliver on average for a miss probability of {{tg}}?
ask.explanation: $e^{-\alpha}$ = {{tg}} gives $\alpha = -\ln({{tg}})$ = **{{-ln(tg)}}** photons per 1 pulse. This is the 'quantum limit' of optical detection: with equally likely bits it averages to about {{-ln(tg)/2}} photons per bit.

steps.prompt: Each transmission attempt of a packet succeeds independently with probability {{q}}. What is the smallest number of attempts $m$ the protocol must allow so that the packet gets through with probability at least {{P}}?
steps.explanation: All $m$ attempts fail with probability $(1-q)^m$, which must be at most $1 - P$ = {{1-P}}. So $m \ge \frac{\ln({{1-P}})}{\ln({{1-q}})}$ = {{ln(1-P)/ln(1-q)}}, and the smallest whole number is **{{ceil(ln(1-P)/ln(1-q)-1e-9)}}**.

steps.prompt: A {{n}}-bit block crosses a channel with bit-error probability {{p}}. Use the Poisson approximation to find the probability that the number of bit errors is exactly {{k}}. (probability, 0–1)
steps.explanation: With $n$ large and $p$ small the error count is nearly Poisson with $\alpha = np$ = {{n*p}}: $P(K = {{k}}) \approx \frac{\alpha^{{{k}}}}{{{k}}!}e^{-\alpha}$ = **{{(n*p)^k*exp(-n*p)/fact(k)}}**. The exact binomial gives {{choose(n,k)*p^k*(1-p)^(n-k)}}.

steps.prompt: Packets arrive as a Poisson stream. Set the expected number of packets per time slot, $\alpha$, so that a slot is empty with probability {{P0}} (dashed line).
steps.explanation: $P(N = 0) = e^{-\alpha}$ = {{P0}} ⇒ $\alpha = -\ln({{P0}})$ = **{{at}}**. Notice how the whole PMF shifts right and spreads out as $\alpha$ grows: its mean and its variance both equal $\alpha$.
